title: Small AI models let drones autonomously identify and attack battlefield targets
content:
As European militaries adapt to the use of AI and drones in modern warfare, a NATO-backed startup is helping to deploy AI-driven target detection and selection that can run on small drones for surveillance and attack missions.
The company Scaleout Systems was originally founded by researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden in 2018, and initially focused on training and deploying machine learning models directly on the hardware available in commercial trucks and other vehicles. But once Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company pivoted toward defense applications.
“With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world, we realized that this technology can be very important to operationalize edge data and sensor data for machine learning to make sure that NATO allies have found that strategic advantage,” Andreas Hellander, cofounder and CEO of Scaleout Systems, told Ars.
Instead of using frontier AI models from OpenAI or Anthropic, Scaleout is harnessing leaner ones, such as machine learning models that can perform computer vision tasks on the hardware of drones or computers used at forward bases. “They need to fit on forward-deployed hardware and edge hardware, which can vary quite a bit from small embedded devices to quite powerful edge workstations,” Hellander said.
Scaleout was selected to join NATO’s Defence Innovator Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) Challenge Program in 2025. There, it has worked on the Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon project to adapt machine learning models for the edge computing hardware found in drones, drone pilot tablets, and field command posts.

report.summary: NATO-backed Scaleout Systems is adapting small edge AI models so drones and field devices can autonomously detect and select battlefield targets.
report.background: Scaleout Systems was founded in 2018 by Uppsala University researchers and initially deployed machine learning on commercial trucks and vehicles. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company pivoted to defense, arguing edge AI could give NATO allies an operational advantage. European militaries are increasingly integrating drones and AI into reconnaissance and strike missions, but frontier models are too large for forward-deployed hardware. Scaleout instead uses lean computer-vision models that run on drones, pilot tablets, and field command posts. In 2025 it joined NATO's DIANA accelerator and began work on the Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon project, adapting models for varied edge devices and disconnected battlefield conditions.
key_points: Scaleout is deliberately avoiding large frontier models from OpenAI or Anthropic. Instead, it uses compact computer-vision models that can run directly on drone hardware, tablets, and forward-base workstations, where compute, power, and connectivity are limited.

The company began with commercial vehicle machine learning, but Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered a defense pivot. Its CEO says the goal is to operationalize edge sensor data so NATO allies gain a strategic advantage in modern warfare.

Scaleout joined NATO's DIANA Challenge Program in 2025 and works on Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon. That project adapts machine learning for drones, pilot tablets, and field command posts, reflecting NATO interest in deployable edge AI.

The system supports target detection and selection for surveillance and attack missions. That raises legal and ethical questions about autonomous targeting, human oversight, and accountability when AI runs on small drones.

Edge deployment offers low latency, works with poor connectivity, and keeps data local. But it also means models must be highly optimized, robust, and adaptable across many different embedded and workstation hardware profiles.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this validates small, efficient edge models as a serious alternative to cloud-based frontier systems, especially in defense, robotics, and industrial settings. Developers will see demand for model quantization, on-device inference, federated learning, and MLOps that works in disconnected or contested environments. Defense-tech careers and dual-use startups may grow, but export controls and ethics reviews will matter. For regular users, the same advances could improve drone inspection, agriculture, search and rescue, and disaster response. Yet cheaper autonomous target detection also accelerates concerns about surveillance, accidental escalation, and accountability for AI-enabled weapons.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch TinyML and TensorFlow Lite Micro for embedded inference, ONNX Runtime for cross-hardware deployment, NVIDIA Jetson for edge AI drones, Edge Impulse for TinyML workflows, YOLO and OpenMMLab for computer vision, Flower for federated learning, and ROS 2 for drone autonomy. These open-source and commercial tools show how small models move from research to real edge devices.
